AgreeLab: AgreeLab help 1/9: Agreement beyond chance
Two raters sort the same N items into k
categories.  Observed agreement po = the
share on the diagonal of the table.
Some agreement happens by chance: if the
raters chose independently at their own
rates, pe = sum of (row share × column share).
Cohen's kappa (1960) = (po - pe)/(1 - pe):
the share of the possible agreement beyond
chance that was reached.  1 = perfect,
0 = chance level, below 0 = worse than chance.
Tiles page: drag a count from an off-diagonal
tile to a diagonal one and watch kappa rise.
Any key or tap = next, ← = back, Esc = leave
AgreeLab help 2/9: SE, CI and the test
Two different SEs (Fleiss, Cohen & Everitt 1969, Psychol Bull
- the large-sample SE gives the 95% CI, kappa ± 1.96 SE (rough
when N is small);
- SE₀, the SE if kappa were 0, gives the test: z = kappa/SE₀,
one-sided p.
p = P(a kappa this big | H₀: kappa = 0).
It is not the chance that H₀ is true, and 'better than chance' is
easy to reach: raters who agree on only 1 item in 3 can reach it.
The CI says how much agreement there is, and how precisely it
is known.
statsmodels' cohens_kappa uses the same SEs.
Any key or tap = next, ← = back, Esc = leave
AgreeLab help 3/9: Kappa max and the paradox
kappa max (Cohen 1960): with these row and
column totals, at most sum of min(row, col)
can agree.  Raters who use the categories at
different rates can never reach kappa = 1.
The paradox (Feinstein & Cicchetti 1990):
high po, low kappa, when one category is
very common: pe is then high too.  Load the
two paradox tables (illustrative numbers):
both have po = 0.85; kappa 0.32 and 0.70.
PABAK = (k po - 1)/(k - 1) (Byrt, Bishop &
Carlin 1993) removes prevalence and bias:
it is po rescaled.  Report po, the margins
and kappa together, not kappa alone.

AgreeLab help 4/9: Weighted kappa
Ordered categories (certain, probable, ...):
a near miss is better than a far one.
Weighted kappa (Cohen 1968) gives tile i, j
the credit w(i, j), 1 on the diagonal:
linear 1 - |i - j|/(k - 1)
(Cicchetti & Allison 1971);
quadratic 1 - (i - j)²/(k - 1)²
(Fleiss & Cohen 1973).
Then po and pe use the weights, and
kappa_w = (po_w - pe_w)/(1 - pe_w); SEs as
for kappa (Fleiss, Cohen & Everitt 1969).
Quadratic weights give the most credit to
near misses.  Choose weights before the data.

AgreeLab help 5/9: Many raters, Fleiss' kappa
Each of N subjects gets m ratings (Fleiss
1971); the raters may differ by subject.
Data: counts n(i, j) = how many put subject i
in category j (each row adds to m).
P_i = share of subject i's m(m-1)/2 rater
pairs that agree; P = their mean.
Pe = sum of p_j², p_j = category j's share.
kappa = (P - Pe)/(1 - Pe); per category too.
SE under H₀ only (Fleiss, Nee & Landis 1979,
Psychol Bull 86:974): a test, but no CI.
Your data: D1-D9 = categories, one row per
subject, every row adding to the same m.

AgreeLab help 6/9: Which ICC?
n targets × k raters, measured values.
ICC = between-target variance / total (Shrout & Fleiss 1979;
McGraw & Wong 1996):
(1,1) different raters for each target;
(2,1) same raters, a sample: ABSOLUTE agreement; a rater who
scores every target higher lowers it;
(3,1) these raters only: CONSISTENCY.
(1,k), (2,k), (3,k): the reliability of the MEAN of the k raters.
CIs from F (S & F 1979; ICC(2,1) with Satterthwaite's df).
Shrout & Fleiss's own example (a preset): .17, .29, .71, .44,
Choose the form from the design, not the value: they answer
different questions.

AgreeLab help 7/9: Bland-Altman
Two methods on the same n targets (Bland & Altman 1986,
Lancet i:307): plot d = A - B against the mean (A + B)/2.
bias =
d
, the mean difference; limits of
agreement = bias ± 1.96 s: about 95% of differences fall there.
CI of the bias: bias ± t s/√n.
CI of a limit: ± t s√(1/n + 1.96²/(2(n - 1))), APPROXIMATE
(Bland & Altman 1986 SE). In a review's simulation (40,000 runs)
it covered about 92% at n = 3-5 and 94% at n = 17.
Trend: regress d on the mean; a slope means the two methods
differ more for larger (or smaller) values.
A high r is not agreement: r ignores bias.

AgreeLab help 8/9: Benchmarks are conventions
Landis & Koch (1977, Biometrics 33:159-174)
offered words for ranges of kappa, as
benchmarks:
below 0 poor, 0 - 0.20 slight,
0.61 - 0.80 substantial,
0.81 - 1 almost perfect.
They are a convention, NOT a test: no
p-value or CI stands behind them, and the
same kappa means different things at other
prevalences or numbers of categories.
Report the kappa, its CI, po and the table.

AgreeLab help 9/9: Agreement and forensic work
Agreement is reliability, not accuracy:
two examiners can agree and both be wrong.
Accuracy needs cases where the truth is
known (ground truth), not a second opinion.
Kappa depends on the mix of cases (the
paradox), so two studies' kappas compare
only if their case mixes are alike.
Kappa assumes independent ratings: a
verifier who knows the first conclusion is
not an independent rater.
A teaching aid only: not validated for
forensic, clinical or legal use.

AnovaLab: AnovaLab help 1/10: What one-way ANOVA asks
H₀: every group has the same population mean μ.
ANOVA splits the total spread (SS) in two:
between: n × (group mean - grand mean)²
within: (value - its own group mean)²
MS = SS / df;  F = MS between / MS within.
If H₀ is true, F is near 1 and follows the
F(k - 1, N - k) curve; p = P(F this big | H₀).
A small p is evidence that SOME mean differs:
not which (Pairs page), not how much (eta²).
eta² = SS between / SS total; omega² (Hays)
subtracts the part chance alone would give.
Every value counts: 0 and negatives are data.

AnovaLab help 2/10: Welch and the checks
The F test assumes equal spreads (and roughly normal groups).
Welch's F (1951) drops equal spreads: each group is weighted
by n / s².
Levene's test (Brown-Forsythe form) runs the one-way F on
|value - group median|; non-normal data affect it little.
Bartlett's χ² compares the s² directly: it is misled by
non-normal data.
In the insect-spray preset, s runs from 1.7 to 6.2 and Levene's
test flags it; compare the ordinary F with Welch's.
A check that is not significant is not proof of equal spreads: with
small groups the checks often miss real differences.
Dots page: look at the spreads yourself.

AnovaLab help 3/10: Which pairs differ?
Many t-tests raise the chance of at least one false alarm; these
keep that chance at α for the whole set (the family):
Tukey-Kramer: q = |diff|/√(MSW/2 (1/n₁+1/n₂)) on the
studentized range (it asks before it runs, since it is slow).
Bonferroni: raw t p × m pairs (simple, safe).
Holm: Bonferroni done in steps; never less power than
Bonferroni.

AnovaLab help 5/10: Dunnett's test
Dunnett's test compares every group with ONE control
group (a placebo, the usual method): k - 1 comparisons,
not all the pairs.  With fewer comparisons, it finds a
real difference more often than Tukey's test does.
t = (group mean - control mean)/SE, SE from MS within
and both n.  A group differs when |t| > d crit, and d crit
keeps the chance of ANY false alarm in the family at α.
Adjusted p: the chance that the LARGEST |t| of the
family is this big when no group differs from the control.
Enter > Dunnett: pick the control.  It asks before it runs
(slow on a G1).  Two pages: the table, then the CIs drawn.
Two-sided; unequal n allowed.  Choose the control before
you see the data.  Dunnett (1955); p within 0.05 %.

AnovaLab help 6/10: Two-way ANOVA
Two factors A and B, every A × B cell filled.
Main effects: do A's (or B's) levels differ?
Interaction: does A's effect depend on B?
Unequal cells (unbalanced): Type III SS, by regression, effect
coding: each effect is tested after all the others.  They need not
add up to the total.  Balanced: classical SS.
Plot: one line per level of the other factor.
Parallel lines = no interaction.  Tap a point for its cell mean and
n; Swap exchanges the two factors in the plot.
Mock-jury preset: unattractive swindlers got 7.0 years on
average, the other cells 3.5 to 4.8; striking, yet the interaction's p
is 0.13 (17 to 21 jurors a cell).

AnovaLab help 7/10: Randomized blocks
Each block (a judge, a person) gets every
treatment once: repeated measures.
Blocks differ a lot, and that spread is taken
OUT of the error: SSE = SST - SSTr - SSBlocks.
F (treatments) = MS treatments / MS error.
partial eta² = SSTr / (SSTr + SSE).
The Table page also shows the one-way F that
ignores the blocks: judges' ratings give
p = 0.048 that way, far smaller with blocks.
Assumes no block × treatment interaction
(and, for repeated measures, sphericity).
Plot: one gray line per block.

AnovaLab help 8/10: One and two variances
One σ: χ² = (n - 1) s² / σ₀², df n - 1.
CI for σ²: ((n-1)s²/χ² upper, (n-1)s²/χ² lower)
Two σ: F = s₁² / s₂², df n₁ - 1 and n₂ - 1.
CI for σ₁²/σ₂²: (F/F upper, F/F lower).
Two-sided p = 2 × the smaller tail.  The curve
shades that tail and the other tail of EQUAL
area (blue), and both critical regions (red).
These tests trust normal data much more than
tests of means do; skewed data mislead them.
For several groups, Levene (Checks) is safer.
Data: type s and n, or pick one-way groups.

BiNorm3D: BiNorm3D help 1/6: What ρ does
X and Y each follow N(0, 1); ρ is their correlation.  The surface is
their joint density f(x, y): the volume under it is 1.
ρ = 0: a round bell.  Knowing X tells you nothing about Y.
ρ > 0: it stretches along y = x (high x with high y); ρ < 0:
along y = −x.
The volume stays 1, so a narrower bell is a taller one: the peak
Color = height: blue low, then magenta, red at the top.  The
height scale never changes, so the peaks can be
compared across ρ.
1/6, tap or key = next page, Esc = back
BiNorm3D help 2/6: Why the contours tilt
Cont looks straight down.  Each ellipse is a
level of the surface, Q = k², where
Q = (x² − 2ρxy + y²) / (1 − ρ²).
The cross term −2ρxy tilts them: along y = x
the variance is 1 + ρ, across it 1 − ρ.
Q is χ² with 2 df, so the share inside
is 1 − e^(−k²/2): 39 % inside k = 1 and
86 % inside k = 2, whatever ρ is.
The magenta line E[Y | x] = ρx is the
regression line.  It runs through the left
and right ends of every ellipse, not along
the long axis.
2/6, tap or key = next page, Esc = back
BiNorm3D help 3/6: What a slice is
Slice cuts the surface along the line x = x₀.
Scaled to area 1, the cut is the distribution
of Y among the cases that have X = x₀:
Y | X = x₀ is N(ρx₀, √(1 − ρ²)).
Its center ρx₀ lies on the regression line
y = ρx; the SD is the same for every x₀.
The ridge of the bell runs along y = x, but
the slices peak on the flatter magenta line.
The panel: f(y | x₀) shaded, N(0, 1) gray for
comparison -- narrower, centered at ρx₀.
Drag the red line, or use Left and Right.
3/6, tap or key = next page, Esc = back
BiNorm3D help 4/6: Regression to the mean
Pick the cases with an extreme x₀, say 2 SD
above the mean.  Their average y is ρx₀:
1.2 SD at ρ = 0.6 -- nearer the mean, though
nothing was done to them.  With |ρ| < 1, ρx₀
is always pulled toward 0; the weaker ρ,
the stronger the pull.
Criminal justice: offenders chosen for a
program because their risk score was
extreme will score closer to the average
next time, program or not.  That drop is
not the program's effect; only a comparison
group picked the same way shows what it added.
4/6, tap or key = next page, Esc = back
BiNorm3D help 5/6: The target and the CEP
CEP shows the pattern from above as a target.  Think of each
(x, y) pair as a shot aimed at the center.
The green circle holds half of all the shots.  Its radius R is the
CEP, the circular error probable: a shot is as likely to land
inside the circle as outside it.  R is in SDs of X (or of Y).
ρ = 0: the pattern is round and R = 1.177.  As ρ moves away
from 0 the pattern grows longer and narrower, and R shrinks:
The blue ellipse holds half of the shots too.  It has the
pattern's own shape, so it covers less area than the circle.
Shots, or a tap on the plot, fires 50 shots and counts those
inside the circle: about half.  Clear removes the shots.

BurrLab: BurrLab help 1/6: The Burr XII model
The Burr XII is a flexible model for a long
right tail: sentences served, waits to
re-arrest, insurance losses, incomes. Two
shapes C and K and a scale S. Its tail is a
power law: P(X > x) falls like x^(-K C).
The mean exists only if K×C > 1, the variance
only if K×C > 2: with a heavy enough tail the
sample mean never settles down to one value
(menu 4).

BurrLab help 3/6: Family tree and fit
Family tree: C = 1 is Pareto II (Lomax); K = 1
is the log-logistic (Fisk); K → ∞ with S = Sw
K^(1/C) is the Weibull. Tap the map to set (C,
K); its colors show whether the mean and the
variance exist there.
Fit: maximum likelihood (a profile Nelder-Mead
over C and S with K solved exactly), SEs from
the observed information, then lognormal,
Weibull, gamma, exponential and Lomax by their
own MLEs, compared by AIC. If the best fit is
at the Weibull or Pareto limit, the fit is
named that.

CICatcher: CICatcher help 1/7: 95 % of WHAT?
Each line is the interval from ONE sample.
The green line is the truth (μ or p): the method never sees it. A
blue line caught it (the interval contains it); a red line missed it.
The 95 % is the share of intervals the METHOD catches in the
long run, not a property of any one interval. Keep adding
samples: the 'all' rate at the top of the screen settles near the
confidence level.
Any one interval either caught μ or missed it.
So say 'we are 95 % confident' -- meaning the method catches
the truth 95 % of the time -- not 'a 95 % chance μ is in
THIS interval'.

CICatcher help 2/7: Level and width; z and t
Drag the right edge (or ⇅): a higher level uses a bigger critical
value, so EVERY line grows, red lines turn blue and the share
caught rises. 99 % catches more, but its longer lines give a less
precise answer.
z:  ± z × σ/√(n) uses the TRUE σ, so every z line has the
same length.
t:  ± t × s/√(n) uses the sample's s.
s changes from sample to sample, so t lines differ in length.
t's critical value is bigger than z's to make up for that:
z with s at n = 10 would catch only 91.8 %.
t critical value: not needed yet (no t run)

CICatcher help 3/7: Wald and Wilson
Wald:  ± z × √((1 - )/n), the textbook interval. Center and
width both come from , which fails when n × p is small:
at p = 0.10, n = 20 Wald catches only 87.6 % (exact binomial; it
claims 95 %).
12.2 % of those samples have  = 0: the Wald interval has ZERO
width and must miss.
Wilson (score) takes its SE from each possible p, not from ,
and keeps every p within z SEs of : never zero width, center
pulled toward 1/2. Same p and n: 95.7 %.
Wald needs n × p and n × (1 - p) to be 10 or more; at p = 0.10,
n = 100 it reaches 93.2 %.
Gray on the axis: impossible values (below 0, above 1). Only
Wald lines can reach them.
any key or tap = next page, Esc = done
CICatcher help 4/7: Exact intervals
Exact (Clopper-Pearson) uses no normal curve:
it keeps every p for which your count is not in either α/2 tail of
Binomial(n, p).
A count has only n + 1 possible values, so no interval can catch
exactly 95 % at every p.
Exact makes sure it is NEVER LESS: at n = 20 its worst case over
every p is 95.8 %.
At p = 0.10, n = 20 it catches 98.9 % (Wilson 95.7 %, Wald 87.6
%); at 80 % or 90 % it still catches 95.7 %. The cost: longer lines
(wider intervals).
0 yeses: from 0 to 1 - (α/2)^(1/n), 0.168 at n = 20 and 95 %.
Tap such a line: the panel shows that end as the CAS writes it.
exact ends: bisection on BINOMIAL_CDF, checked

CICatcher help 5/7: Tolerance intervals
A confidence interval is about a mean.  A tolerance interval is
about single values:  ± k s is made to hold at least 90 % (or
95 %, or 99 %) of the whole population.
The green band is the middle 90 % of the population.  A blue
line holds at least 90 % of the population; a red line holds less.
Tap a line: the panel says how much of the population it holds.
The level is the share of samples whose line holds its 90 %:
the 'all' rate at the top settles near it.
k is larger than z = 1.645 because  and s are estimates: at
n = 10 and 95 %, k = 2.856.  k is worked out exactly here;
printed tables often give an approximation that differs in the
third digit.

CICatcher help 6/7: A criminal-justice example
A city asks n = 100 residents: 'Are you afraid
to walk alone at night?' 38 say yes, so
 = 0.38 and the 95 % Wald interval is
RIGHT: 'We are 95 % confident the true share
is between 28.5 % and 47.5 %': the method
catches the truth 95 % of the time.
WRONG: 'There is a 95 % chance the true share
is in this interval.' The share is fixed;
this interval caught it or it did not.

predicts (χ², Benford, Poisson, binomial)?
NORMALITY: could a sample have come from a
normal distribution (Q-Q plot, W, A², D, χ² on
bins)?  And the exact binomial test for one
proportion, and Dixon's test for one outlier
in a small sample.

FitCheck help 2/12: Goodness of fit
χ² GOODNESS OF FIT.  E = N × (the cell's
proportion under H₀): what the cell would hold
if H₀ were exactly right.  χ² = sum of (O -
E)²/E: big when the counts are far from E.  df
= k - 1 - m, where m counts the parameters
estimated from the same data (Poisson λ: 1;
binomial p: 1; normal μ and σ: 2).  p = the
right tail of the χ² curve (Curve page).
Each cell's contribution (O - E)²/E is the
magenta strip under the bars; (O - E)/√E is
its signed square root: beyond ±2 the cell
stands out.

FitCheck help 3/12: Small counts and Merge
The χ² curve gives a trustworthy p only when
the E are not too small: every E ≥ 5, or
Cochran's rule (at most 20% of the E below 5
and none below 1).  FitCheck checks EVERY
cell.  If the rule fails, Merge joins
neighboring cells, the smallest E first, and
the Test page names exactly which cells were

FitCheck help 7/12: Outliers: Dixon's test
DIXON'S OUTLIER TEST (the Outlier key; 3 to 30
values).  Is the lowest or the highest value
too far from the rest to come from the same
normal population?  Sort the values: x(1) is
the lowest, x(n) the highest.  The ratio is a
gap over a range: how far the value stands
from its neighbor, as a share of the spread.
0 = no gap; 1 = it stands alone.
The page draws every value as a dot, the
tested one in red, with its gap (red) and its
range (blue) above the dots.  It tests the end
with the bigger ratio.

FitCheck help 8/12: Outliers: which ratio
The ratio changes with n (Dixon 1953).  First
digit: the gap ends at the nearest value (1)
or the second-nearest (2).  Second digit: how
many values the range leaves off its far end.
3 to 7 values: r₁₀.  The gap to the nearest
value, over the whole range.
8 to 10: r₁₁.  The range leaves off 1 value.
11 to 13: r₂₁.  The gap to the second-nearest
value; the range leaves off 1.
14 to 30: r₂₂.  The range leaves off 2 values.
Why: a second outlier, beside the first or at
the far end, would hide the first.  The later
ratios guard against that.

FitCheck help 9/12: Outliers: the p and its limits
THE P is the chance, in a normal sample of
this size, of a ratio this big or bigger at
that end.  FitCheck computes it; a printed
table of critical values can differ from it in
the third decimal (McBane 2006).
The test takes the end with the bigger ratio,
so the p it reports is for either end: twice
the one-end p, as in the printed tables.  That
is an upper limit.
A small p is a reason to check the value: was
it misread, mistyped, or from another
population?  It is no license to delete it.
The p assumes normal data (see the Q-Q plot).
Values tied by rounding can make the ratio 1.

RankLab: RankLab help 1/10: What it does
Rank tests replace each value by its rank, so an outlier counts no
more than the next value, and no normal population is assumed.
Tied values share the average of the ranks they span: the
MIDRANK.  Every test here uses midranks and the
tie-corrected variance.

picture, the null distribution (and Dunn pairs for Kruskal-
Wallis).  Soft keys: Result, Plot, Null, the 4th key (Exact/Normal,
or what that page switches), Tails, More (Help, Dunn or
Data, Menu).

RankLab help 3/10: Sign test, signed-rank
Both test H₀: the median of d is 0.  Zeros
are dropped: n counts the nonzero d only.
SIGN: S+ = number of d > 0, Binomial(n, 1/2)
under H₀; exact p from BINOMIAL_CDF; two-
sided = 2 × the smaller tail (at most 1).
SIGNED-RANK: rank |d| (midranks); T+ = the
sum of the ranks of d > 0.  Under H₀ each
sign is + or - with chance 1/2, 2^n patterns;
RankLab counts them all (ties too), n ≤ 50.
Effect r = (T+ - T-)/(n(n+1)/2).  Estimate:
Hodges-Lehmann = the median of all Walsh
averages (d_i + d_j)/2, i ≤ j (n ≤ 100).

RankLab help 4/10: Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis
MANN-WHITNEY: rank both groups together;
U₁ = R₁ - n₁(n₁ + 1)/2 = the (X, Y) pairs with
X > Y (ties count 1/2).  Exact: every split
of the N ranks is equally likely; RankLab
counts them (no ties, n₁ n₂ ≤ 400).  Ties:
normal, tie-corrected, continuity corrected.
P(X > Y) + ties/2 = U₁/(n₁ n₂); rank-biserial
r = (U₁ - U₂)/(n₁ n₂).  Hodges-Lehmann shift.
KRUSKAL-WALLIS: H compares the k mean ranks;
p from χ²(k - 1); epsilon² = H/(N - 1).
DUNN: z for each pair of mean ranks, Holm-
adjusted over the k(k - 1)/2 pairs.

RankLab help 6/10: Page's L, an ordered trend
Friedman asks whether the treatments differ at all.  PAGE'S L
asks more: do they rise in the ORDER LISTED (column 1, 2, 3 ...)?
Rank within each block (row), as Friedman does.  Then
L = 1 × R₁ + 2 × R₂ + ... + k × Rk     (R = a column's rank sum)
A block whose ranks follow the order adds the most to L.

order and the direction BEFORE you see the data.

up to 77 blocks; 5: 17; 9: 3; fewer with ties), ties as they are.
NORMAL: z = (L - mean)/SD, with no continuity correction.

RankLab help 7/10: The runs test
THE RUNS TEST asks whether the ORDER of a sequence is
random.  It is not a rank test: it only counts.  A RUN is a
stretch of the same kind:  R R R R B R R R  has 3 runs.
Two kinds (red or black, pass or fail) are used as they are.
Numbers are cut at their median into above and below; a value
equal to the median is dropped.
TOO FEW runs: like values cluster (a drift, a trend, streaks).
TOO MANY runs: the two kinds alternate more than chance does.
Tails: lower = too few, upper = too many, two-sided = either.
EXACT p: every order of the two kinds is equally likely under
H₀; RankLab counts the orders (n ≤ 2,000).
NORMAL: z = (runs - mean)/SD, mean = 2 n₁ n₂/n + 1.
Plot: a square for each value; numbers also as a chart (More).

EXACT: p from the statistic's whole null distribution, counted.
NORMAL: z with the continuity correction (0.5 toward the mean)
and, with ties, the tie-corrected variance.
(Page's L and the runs test: z without that correction.)

A p-value is P(a statistic this extreme | H₀), not the chance that

RiskLab: RiskLab help 1/8: Logistic regression
A risk tool turns facts about a person into a
score that predicts an outcome Y (1 = re-
arrested, 0 = not).  Logistic regression:
ln(P/(1 - P)) = b₀ + b₁x₁ + ... + bk xk
odds = P/(1 - P); OR = e^b multiplies the odds
for +1 in x, the other x held fixed.
Fit: Newton-Raphson (IRLS), b → b + I^-1 U,
U = X'(y - μ), I = X'WX, W = μ(1 - μ),
until each step < 1E-9 (Hosmer & Lemeshow
2000; Agresti 2013).  SE = √(diag. of I^-1).
Wald z = b/SE.  LR χ² = 2(lnL - lnL₀), df k.
McFadden R² = 1 - lnL/lnL₀ (McFadden 1974):
not a share of variance explained.

RiskLab help 2/8: Separation, collinearity
If some x (or a mix of x) puts every Y = 1 above every Y = 0, the
likelihood keeps rising as |b| grows: no finite estimate
(Albert & Anderson 1984).  RiskLab warns when the fit has not
converged in 25 steps, the fitted line orders Y perfectly, or I
turns singular.  Remedies: drop or merge that x, or a penalized
(Firth) fit, not offered here.
Collinear x (one a mix of the others) make I singular too: no SEs.
Speed: each step of the fit goes through every row; Rossi's 432
rows need about 7 passes.  On a G1 that is slow (a progress bar
shows it; Esc stops it).

RiskLab help 3/8: The ROC curve and the AUC
Flag 'high risk' if the score ≥ a cut-off.
TPR (sensitivity) = flagged share of Y = 1;
FPR = 1 - specificity = flagged share of Y=0.
Moving the cut-off from high to low traces the
ROC curve from (0, 0) to (1, 1); tied scores
make a diagonal step.  AUC = area under it =
P(a random Y = 1 scores above a random Y = 0),
ties 1/2: the Mann-Whitney U/(n₁ n₀).
0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect.  SE: DeLong et al.
(1988); CI = AUC ± 1.96 SE, cut at 0 and 1.
Tap the AUC line: Hanley-McNeil's SE (1982),
which assumes a shape; DeLong's does not.
A model's AUC on its own data is optimistic.

RiskLab help 4/8: Cut-offs and trade-offs
A lower cut-off flags more people: more TP (sensitivity up) and
more FP (specificity down).  No cut-off avoids both errors.
PPV = TP/(TP + FP): of those flagged, the share with Y = 1.  It
depends on the base rate: the same sensitivity and specificity
give a lower PPV where Y = 1 is rarer.
NPV = TN/(TN + FN).
Choosing a cut-off is choosing which error matters more: the
statistics show the trade-off, but they cannot say which error
is worse.
COMPAS deciles: 1-4 low, 5-7 medium, 8-10 high; ProPublica
took 5 and up as high risk.

RiskLab help 5/8: Calibration, H-L test
Calibrated: of people given P = 0.3, about 30% have Y = 1.
RiskLab sorts by predicted P into 10 groups (ties kept together),
or one group per score level, and compares observed O with
expected E = sum of P in each group:
HL = sum of (O - E)²/(E(1 - E/n)), df = groups - 2
(Hosmer & Lemeshow 1980).  Weaknesses: it depends on the
number of groups and on how ties are cut (software differs); it
has low power with small n, and with large n a tiny misfit is
'significant' (Hosmer et al. 1997).
A large p is no proof of good calibration.
Gray bars: pred ± 1.96 SE, a rough guide.
For a score such as COMPAS's, pred is the P from RiskLab's own
logistic fit of Y on the score.

RiskLab help 6/8: Fairness definitions
Predictive parity: the same score means the same risk in both
groups, so PPV is equal (Northpointe: Dieterich et al. 2016, with
equal AUC, 'accuracy equity').
Error-rate balance: equal FPR and equal FNR in both groups
(ProPublica: Angwin et al.
2016).  When base rates differ and prediction is not perfect,
these cannot all hold at once:
Chouldechova (2017) for PPV, FPR and FNR;
Kleinberg, Mullainathan & Raghavan (2016) for calibration vs
equal average scores among Y=1 and among Y=0.  Both sides'
numbers can be right at once, because they answer different
questions.
